nameStory: The Asiatic dayflower gets its name because each delicate bloom lasts for just one day before wilting away. In its native China, people call it 'duckfoot herb' because of the shape of its leaves, while in Japan it's known as 'dew herb' - perhaps because the flowers are so ephemeral they seem as fleeting as morning dew.
description: Asiatic dayflower is a low-growing annual plant that spreads along the ground with trailing stems that can root at the joints. It produces charming but short-lived flowers with two bright blue petals and one tiny white petal that emerge from a folded leaf-like bract. The plant typically grows 6-12 inches tall but can spread several feet wide, forming loose mats in disturbed areas and gardens. Originally from East Asia, it has become a common naturalized plant throughout much of New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Distinctive three-petaled flowers with two large, bright blue petals above and one small, inconspicuous white petal below, emerging from a folded green bract that looks like a taco shell

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Smooth, lance-shaped leaves that feel slightly succulent and wrap around the stem at their base, with parallel veins running lengthwise like grass

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, sprawling stems that trail along the ground and often root where they touch soil, creating spreading patches rather than upright clumps

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, jointed stems that feel somewhat fleshy and break easily, often with a slightly zigzag pattern between the leaf joints

idTips.label: Flower Timing
idTips.description: Flowers open in the morning and close by afternoon of the same day, so you'll only see them blooming in the earlier part of the day

habitat: Look for Asiatic dayflower in disturbed soils, gardens, roadsides, and waste areas throughout New England, especially in moist, rich soil. It thrives in partially shaded spots like the edges of woodlands, around buildings, and in cultivated areas where the soil has been turned over. You'll often find it mixed with other weedy plants in areas that get some foot traffic or periodic disturbance.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as the weather warms, initially forming small rosettes of smooth, grass-like leaves before the trailing stems begin to develop.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with the distinctive blue and white flowers opening each morning from summer into early fall. The sprawling stems are most noticeable now as they spread and root.
seasonality.fall: Flowering continues into early fall until the first frost, when the entire plant dies back. Seeds are produced in small capsules throughout the growing season.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain - this annual plant survives only as seeds in the soil, waiting for warm weather to return.

funFact: The blue petals of Asiatic dayflower were used to create a special dye for the famous Japanese woodblock prints (ukiyo-e) of the 18th and 19th centuries - the same vivid blue you see in classic works by artists like Hokusai was literally squeezed from these humble weedy flowers!
confusionNotes: The unique flower structure with two blue petals and one white petal makes this plant nearly impossible to confuse with anything else when in bloom. When not flowering, the smooth, grass-like leaves might be mistaken for young grass shoots, but dayflower leaves wrap around the stem at their base and feel slightly thick and succulent.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'weed' in North America, this plant has a rich cultural history in its native Asia, where it's been used in traditional medicine for centuries. The scientific name Commelina honors two Dutch botanist brothers - Linnaeus used the two large petals to represent the two accomplished brothers, while the tiny third petal represented a third brother who was less notable in botany.
compareHints: Asiatic dayflower is the only member of its genus commonly found in New England, making it unique in the region. The closest relatives you might encounter are other members of the spiderwort family, but Virginia spiderwort has three equal-sized petals (usually purple) and grows much taller and more upright. The grass-like leaves and trailing growth habit of dayflower are quite distinctive within this plant family.
